summary:
With recent data released from NASA’s SPHEREx mission, we developed SATE: an accessible website for the public to visualise the satellite’s infrared observations. We aim to empower the public to participate in astronomical discovery. In particular, our app will be useful for tracking the motion of celestial bodies and discovering previously undetected objects. 

Users can select a particular region to investigate, either through navigating our easy to use sky map or selecting Right Ascension and Declination coordinates. Afterwards, users can compare images captured at different times to identify changes in the positions of celestial objects. Alternatively, users can explore the region across different infrared wavelengths, taking advantage of SPHEREx's 102 spectral bands.
 
Our app will also allow users to volunteer their GPU power and spare LLM tokens to accelerate the discovery process. These computational resources will cross-reference SPHEREx observations against existing catalogues of known celestial objects to identify discrepancies and potential candidates for undiscovered objects.
details:
How it works

SATE is an interactive web application that makes NASA's SPHEREx infrared observations accessible to the public, facilitating the tracking of celestial objects and identification of potentially undiscovered objects. Users can explore the celestial sphere through our interactive sky map or enter specific Right Ascension and Declination coordinates. Once a region is selected, users can compare observations captured at different times to identify changes in celestial objects' positions or explore SPHEREx's 102 infrared spectral bands. SATE also aims to incorporate a community-powered discovery system, allowing users to contribute spare GPU computing power and unused LLM tokens to cross-reference observations against existing astronomical catalogues and identify potential discoveries.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Despite NASA's publicly available astronomical datasets, their technical complexity and computational demands can limit public participation. SATE addresses these barriers through an intuitive interface that allows anyone, regardless of scientific background, to explore real astronomical observations. Our proposed volunteer computing system further transforms users into active contributors, pooling computational resources to accelerate astronomical analysis.

Creativity and Innovation

SATE's innovation lies in combining three complementary approaches to astronomical exploration: interactive sky visualisation, temporal and spectral comparison, and crowdsourced computational analysis.

Rather than simply displaying astronomical imagery, SATE aims to provide tools that allow users to investigate observations and identify scientifically interesting changes. The integration of volunteer GPU computing and LLM-assisted analysis further distinguishes our approach, creating opportunities for collaborative astronomical discovery.

This combination of public accessibility and distributed analysis allows SATE to function as both an educational resource and a potential tool for scientific investigation.

Technical Development

The SATE website uses JavaScript, HTML and CSS with a Node.js backend, hosted on Vercel. We display the sky map using Aladin Lite, and HEALPix divides it into searchable regions. SphereX observations are retrieved from NASA/IPAC IRSA APIs, using custom JavaScript to read FITS data.

Testing and evidence

We tested SATE using real SPHEREx observations of known objects. Our 3I/ATLAS demonstration follows the comet through 11 observations on 14 December 2025, showing approximately 9.58 arcminutes of motion over 3.29 hours.

We also compared matched infrared samples of the known variable star J1502099+593125 across two observing periods. Its background-subtracted image signal decreased by approximately 79%, while two comparison patches remained close to their earlier values. Both images use the same display scale and common quality mask. This demonstrates visible brightness change rather than precision photometry or an occultation detection.

Our supporting evidence includes images, observation identifiers, methods, and outcomes for the five targets named in the challenge.

View our testing results and supporting evidence:
https://drive.google.com/file/d/1zcQPRVOPJGxJIKmaV8GG072ipVj5v21d/view

Design Considerations and Challenges

Throughout development, we prioritised accessibility, scientific accuracy, computational efficiency, and scalability. Our interface aims to accommodate users without specialised astronomical knowledge, while accounting for observational differences, image alignment, and catalogue limitations to ensure scientifically meaningful results. Given the computational demands of large astronomical datasets, we also considered efficient processing and distributed computing. Finally, we designed SATE with future expansion in mind, allowing for additional datasets and more sophisticated detection methods.
